newsitem.title: CHINA: China looks to boost diesel output as demand rises.
newsitem.headline: China looks to boost diesel output as demand rises.

text.p: China wants to expand its output of diesel fuel to try to keep up with expected sharp growth in demand from transport and agriculture, Chinese oil officials said on Tuesday.
China also wants to boost diesel output relative to petrol production at domestic refineries, raising the diesel-to-gasoline ratio to 1.45 to 1.0 from the current 1.2 to 1.0, they said.

Apparent annual demand for diesel was expected to reach 55.7-56.7 million tonnes in 2000 compared with 41.6 million tonnes a year in 1995, said Han Jingcheng, senior engineer at China Petrochemical Consulting Corp, a subsidiary of state-run refiner Sinopec.
He forecast gasoline demand climbing to 36.06-36.75 million tonnes in 2000 from 26.3 million tonnes in 1995.
That takes into account domestic production and net imports but does not make adjustments for inventory changes, he said.
"We see a large rise in demand for diesel," he told Reuters at an oil conference.
"The large scale of our road construction is a major factor," he said, adding that diesel-engine trucks would be the key sources of expanded transport demand.

China once relied heavily on rail transport but has been building modern highways at a rapid pace, and that has been accompanied by a steep rise in the number of trucks, buses and cars in use around the country.
Increasingly mechanised agriculture is another major contributor, while electric power generation, particularly in southern China, was also likely to play a role in the expanded use of diesel.
Su Yimin, senior engineer at Sinopec's Petrochemical Planning and Engineering Institute, echoed that assessment of the future need for more diesel in the product mix.
"We have too much gasoline" relative to diesel, she told Reuters.
China's imports also would probably reflect the shift in the rise in diesel demand although Sinopec officials said they wanted to encourage domestic production.
They said slimmer profit margins for diesel as compared to gasoline were another factor holding back a switch to diesel. Pricing policies had to be adjusted to encourage diesel output, they said.
